cards.explanation: The answer is his own. The verse says the man who isolates himself "…pursues selfish desires…" and the whole picture is one guy, one wish list (Proverbs 18:1). Nobody else gets a vote in that house. I spent years in a drawer with nobody to ask what I wanted, and I'm telling you, friends, it did NOT make me wiser.

The answer is False. Proverbs 18:1 says the man who isolates himself "…rebels against all sound judgment." Going along with it would be the other direction entirely. I think when nobody's around to say "hey, maybe not," that rebelling gets real easy.

The answer is airing his opinions. The fool "…does not delight in understanding, but only in airing his opinions" (Proverbs 18:2). Understanding means taking something in, and he's all about sending his own stuff out. Friends, he's a mixer with no bowl, just spinning.
The answer is contempt. "With a wicked man comes contempt as well…" (Proverbs 18:3). Notice the "as well." The wicked man doesn't show up alone, friends, he drags something along with him.

The answer is the fountain of wisdom. The verse says "the fountain of wisdom is a bubbling brook" (Proverbs 18:4). So the verse sets two pictures of water side by side: a man's words as deep waters, and wisdom as a bubbling brook. I think a brook that keeps bubbling is a nice picture of wisdom that doesn't run dry.

The answer is True. The verse says showing partiality to the wicked is not good, "…nor is depriving the innocent of justice" (Proverbs 18:5). So it names both as not good, friends. One is showing partiality to the wicked, and the other is depriving the innocent of justice.

The answer is strife. "A fool’s lips bring him strife…" (Proverbs 18:6). He opens his mouth and trouble walks right in. I think we all know somebody who could've skipped a whole week of drama by just not replying.

The answer is True. "A fool’s mouth is his ruin, and his lips are a snare to his soul" (Proverbs 18:7). A snare is a trap, friends, and the verse puts that trap on his own lips. That's a lot of trouble for one pair of lips.
The answer is down into the inmost being. The gossip's words "…go down into the inmost being" (Proverbs 18:8). I think that's why they stick, friends. A morsel goes down, and then it stays with you.

The answer is destroys. The man slothful in his work is "…brother to him who destroys" (Proverbs 18:9). Sitting on the job and tearing things down are called family, friends. A lazy man might not swing the hammer, but the verse still hands him the family name.

The answer is that they run to it and are safe. "The name of the LORD is a strong tower; the righteous run to it and are safe" (Proverbs 18:10). They run, friends, no strolling and no browsing. And the ones who run to it are the ones who end up safe.

The answer is in his imagination. The rich man's wealth is "…like a high wall in his imagination" (Proverbs 18:11). The wall is real to him, but the verse puts it in his head. Compare that to verse 10, friends, where the tower is the name of the LORD.

The answer is proud. "Before his downfall a man’s heart is proud…" (Proverbs 18:12). Pride shows up first and the fall comes after. Humility is the other direction, friends: it "…comes before honor." Two paths in one verse.

The answer is humility. "…humility comes before honor" (Proverbs 18:12). Pride goes in front of a fall, and humility goes in front of honor. Same verse, two roads, friends. I'll gladly take the second line.

The answer is True. Proverbs 18:13 says "He who answers a matter before he hears it" and then calls it "…folly and disgrace to him." Answering first and listening later gets a double label, friends. It's both folly and disgrace. Hear first, then answer.

The answer is False. The verse says a man's spirit can endure sickness, then asks, "…who can survive a broken spirit?" (Proverbs 18:14). So it's not called easy at all. I think this one hurts a little, friends, and it's good to slow down for it.

The answer is that they go after it. "The heart of the discerning acquires knowledge, and the ear of the wise seeks it out" (Proverbs 18:15). Seeks it out is the key, friends. Wise folks go on a hunt, they don't wait for it to knock. The discerning and the wise are on the same job.

The answer is True. "A man’s gift opens doors for him, and brings him before great men" (Proverbs 18:16). Both halves are in the verse, friends. The gift opens the door, and then it brings the man before great men. That's a lot of work for one gift.

The answer is that another comes and cross-examines him. "The first to state his case seems right until another comes and cross-examines him" (Proverbs 18:17). It says seems, friends. The other side comes with questions, and the first story gets tested.

The answer is that it separates strong opponents. "Casting the lot ends quarrels and separates strong opponents" (Proverbs 18:18). It does two jobs in one line, friends. The fight ends, and the two strong sides get pulled apart. That's a handy thing to have in a quarrel.

The answer is False. "An offended brother is harder to win than a fortified city…" (Proverbs 18:19). Harder, not easier, friends. And the verse adds that disputes are "…like the bars of a castle." Walls and bars in one verse.

The answer is True. "From the fruit of his mouth a man’s belly is filled…" (Proverbs 18:20). Words are talked about like a crop, friends. What you speak is what you end up eating. That's a good reason to watch what comes off the lips.

The answer is death. "Life and death are in the power of the tongue…" (Proverbs 18:21). Both are in there, life and death. That's a lot of weight for something so small, friends. And the verse puts it on the tongue.

The answer is True, because Proverbs 18:21 says "…those who love it will eat its fruit." That ties right back to verse 20, friends, with the same crop picture. Love the tongue, and you eat what it grows, so plant carefully.

The answer is favor from the LORD. The verse puts both in one line: "He who finds a wife finds a good thing and obtains favor from the LORD" (Proverbs 18:22). The extra blessing is favor from the LORD, friends. That makes two blessings in one verse.

The answer is harshly. "The poor man pleads for mercy, but the rich man answers harshly" (Proverbs 18:23). The verse sets the two side by side, friends. One pleads for mercy, and the other answers harshly. I think this one stings a little.

The answer is one friend who stays closer than a brother. The verse says "A man of many companions may come to ruin, but there is a friend who stays closer than a brother" (Proverbs 18:24). It puts one true friend up against a whole crowd, friends. I'd take that one friend.
